revisions.body: Eryximachus turns a fatigued drinking party into a different kind of gathering. After the company settles that no one must drink heavily, he immediately proposes sending the aulos-girl away and replacing her music with shared speeches. The important move is not simply that conversation begins; it is that the evening’s form is renegotiated in public, with consent marking the passage from bodily recovery to collective verbal performance. I read this as the dialogue making its own change of medium audible.

At the conclusion, Eryximachus gives the whole of Eros “all” power, yet reserves the greatest power for the Eros ordered toward goods with moderation and justice. Does his praise finally embrace love in general, or depend on a disciplined selection within it?

Agathon changes the terms of the encomium before supplying his portrait. He says, in his own assessment, that the earlier speakers praised the benefits Eros brings rather than Eros himself, and proposes a sequence: first describe what Eros is, then what he causes. The passage gives us a standard Agathon announces, not a verdict that the evening has been corrected. Its interest lies in the test he now sets for his own speech: can the portrait that follows meet the method he has just declared?

Diotima asks Socrates to follow a method, and the method matters here more than any retrospective catalogue of the evening’s loves. The ascent moves from one beautiful body to two and then to all beautiful bodies, from bodies to practices and learnings, and finally to learning concerned with Beauty itself. The passage then presents Beauty itself in terms of permanence and independence, before linking its vision to true virtue. One may read earlier speeches against these rungs, but this text leaves that mapping interpretive rather than promising it.
The scene receives Alcibiades first as sound, not sight: his voice announces the new witness before the witness can speak, making his entrance a disturbance before it becomes an argument.
I read the oversized cup as a comic measure of control: Alcibiades can appoint himself ruler of the drinking, but his show of command cannot make Socrates drunk.
I hear a productive mismatch here: Eryximachus preserves the public turn about Eros, while Alcibiades uses it to stage a personal reckoning with Socrates.

I read the story's central inversion this way: Alcibiades explicitly casts himself as a lover plotting against a beloved. He escalates from private exercise to dinner and an overnight stay, yet Socrates resists; Alcibiades reports waking beside him as if beside a father or elder brother. The failed seduction opens the Silenus figure from another angle: desire meets an interior that will not be possessed.
